highlights: Japan enforced the 4 January purge directives, disqualifying roughly 90 percent of former Diet members and dissolving 120 ultranationalist organizations, while general elections were postponed from 21 March to 10 April 1946 for candidate screening.

The Supreme Commander appointed nine judges to the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, with Sir William Flood Webb of Australia as President; 81 war crime suspects were apprehended and Yokohama trials began.

Emergency Imperial ordinances blocked bank deposits, converted old yen currency, and authorized compulsory expropriation of hoarded staple foods (Ordinance No. 66) amid rampant inflation and critical food shortages.
The 1945-46 rice collection reached only 50 percent of quota, while February coal production reached 1,364,000 metric tons and railway deficits prompted rate increases of 250 to 300 percent.
Procedural regulations for the Labor Union Law were promulgated as union membership approached one million, and the cabinet debated workers' 'production control' strikes.
Japan abolished licensed prostitution and nullified contracts between prostitutes and managers; mass DDT dusting was used against a major typhus outbreak in Osaka.
USAMGIK established the Representative Democratic Council under Syngman Rhee, regulated political parties under Ordinance No. 55, and began compulsory rice collection under Ordinance No. 45.
U.S. and Soviet commanders concluded initial interzone agreements on transportation and communication, while Korea faced fertilizer shortages after the cutoff from North Korea.

summary: Summation No. 5 covers non-military activities of the Allied occupation in Japan and the U.S. Army Military Government in Korea (USAMGIK) during February 1946. In Japan, SCAP and the Shidehara Cabinet vigorously enforced the 4 January purge directives, disqualifying roughly 90 percent of former Diet members and dissolving 120 ultranationalist organizations, while postponing national elections to 10 April. Confronting rampant inflation and critical food shortages, the Japanese government promulgated emergency ordinances blocking bank deposits, mandating currency conversion, expropriating hoarded staple crops, and establishing price controls. Meanwhile, labor unions gained legal recognition under the new Labor Union Law, with membership approaching one million, as workers increasingly deployed 'production control' strikes. In social affairs, SCAP directed the abolition of licensed prostitution, implemented mass typhus control in Osaka, and expanded democratic media dissemination. In southern Korea, USAMGIK established the Representative Democratic Council headed by Syngman Rhee, enacted strict regulations on political parties, instituted forced rice collections, and concluded initial interzone administrative agreements with Soviet authorities. For historians, this report provides invaluable contemporary statistical data and policy documentation detailing the structural democratization, economic crises, and institutional transitions across postwar Japan and Korea.
